title: Life-threatening acute asthma

card.complaint: Wheezy and too breathless to finish a sentence

triage.note: Known asthmatic. Two days of a cold, then worsening wheeze today. Her blue inhaler has not helped despite 20 puffs. Came by auto-rickshaw with her roommate.

speech.impairedText: (She shakes her head. Too breathless to speak.)

appearance.text: Much more comfortable. Talking in full sentences.
Wheezy, sitting forward, speaking in short sentences.
Exhausted, speaking single words, using accessory muscles.
Drowsy, slumping, very little chest movement: a silent chest.

history.q: How much reliever have you used?
Ever been in ICU or on a ventilator for asthma?
Do you use a preventer inhaler?

history.a: She’s been getting worse all afternoon. She stopped taking her brown inhaler because she ran out, and she was in intensive care two years ago with this.

exam.label: Chest
exam.text: Hyperexpanded chest, widespread polyphonic wheeze, reduced air entry bilaterally. Trachea central, equal expansion.

variants.text: Very quiet chest: barely any air entry or wheeze (silent chest). Trachea central.
Scattered expiratory wheeze only. Good air entry.

exam.label: General
exam.text: Sitting forward, using accessory muscles, speaking in single words.

variants.text: Drowsy and exhausted: a sign of imminent respiratory arrest.

investigations.label: Peak expiratory flow
investigations.text: PEF 130 L/min (≈ 30% of best 430 L/min): life-threatening range (< 33%).

investigations.label: Arterial blood gas (on oxygen)
investigations.text: pH 7.36, pO₂ 9.1 kPa (68 mmHg), pCO₂ 5.6 kPa (42 mmHg), HCO₃⁻ 23, lactate 2.4. A NORMAL pCO₂ in a breathless asthmatic is a life-threatening feature.

variants.text: pH 7.24, pO₂ 7.9 kPa (59 mmHg), pCO₂ 7.4 kPa (56 mmHg): rising CO₂, near-fatal asthma.
pH 7.45, pO₂ 13 kPa (98 mmHg), pCO₂ 4.2 kPa (32 mmHg).

investigations.label: Potassium (on gas)
investigations.text: K⁺ 3.2 mmol/L: low, as expected with repeated β₂-agonists.

interventions.label: Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 20 min
Aminophylline IV loading dose
interventions.feedback: Only after senior discussion. There is little evidence of benefit over nebulised bronchodilators and there are more side effects (arrhythmias, vomiting).

harm.why: Sedatives are contraindicated in acute asthma: they suppress respiratory drive and can precipitate respiratory arrest.

interventions.label: Amoxicillin 500 mg oral
interventions.feedback: Antibiotics are not routinely indicated in acute asthma; most exacerbations are viral.

interventions.label: Call ICU / anaesthetist
interventions.say: Nurse: “ICU registrar and anaesthetist are coming.”

interventions.label: RSI and intubation (anaesthetist)
interventions.feedback: Intubation is for exhaustion, rising CO₂, drowsiness or arrest despite maximal treatment, done by the most experienced person available.

dispositions.label: Discharge once PEF improves, with oral steroids

critical.label: Nebulised salbutamol
critical.why: High-dose inhaled β₂-agonist is first-line, repeated back-to-back in severe attacks.

critical.label: Oxygen to target 94–98%
critical.why: Hypoxaemia with SpO₂ < 92% is a life-threatening feature.

critical.label: Systemic steroid
critical.why: Steroids reduce mortality and relapse; give them early.

critical.label: Escalated to ICU / anaesthetist
critical.why: Life-threatening features (PEF < 33%, SpO₂ < 92%, normal or rising pCO₂, silent chest, exhaustion) need early critical-care involvement.

teaching: Severity: acute severe = PEF 33–50%, RR ≥ 25, HR ≥ 110, unable to complete sentences. Life-threatening = PEF < 33%, SpO₂ < 92%, normal pCO₂, silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion, altered consciousness, hypotension or arrhythmia.
A normal pCO₂ in a breathless asthmatic means she is tiring. A rising pCO₂ means near-fatal asthma.
Give oxygen to 94–98%, oxygen-driven nebulised salbutamol 5 mg (back-to-back if severe), ipratropium 0.5 mg, and prednisolone 40–50 mg or IV hydrocortisone 100 mg.
Consider IV magnesium sulfate 1.2–2 g over 20 minutes for acute severe asthma not responding to initial treatment.
Never sedate a patient with acute asthma outside a critical-care setting.
Previous ICU admission, non-adherence to preventer therapy and heavy reliever use predict fatal asthma.
Chest X-ray is not routine: do it if pneumothorax, consolidation or a life-threatening attack is suspected, without delaying treatment.
references: BTS/NICE/SIGN. Asthma: diagnosis, monitoring and chronic asthma management (2024), and BTS/SIGN acute asthma guidance.
